core_summary: This chapter presents the principles of electric current, electric potential, and electric circuits. It details Ohm's Law establishing the linear relationship between voltage and current across a conductor. It analyzes electrical resistance, factors influencing resistivity, and mathematical rules for resistors connected in series and parallel combinations. Finally, it explores Joule's Law of heating, domestic heating appliances, electric fuse protection, and electric power calculations.
key_concepts: Electric Current (I = Q/t) as net rate of charge flow through a conductor, measured in Amperes (A); electron flow opposite to conventional current direction
Electric Potential and Potential Difference (V = W/Q) maintained across a circuit by chemical cells, measured in Volts (V)
Ohm's Law: V = IR; Potential difference across a metallic conductor is directly proportional to current flowing through it at constant temperature
Electrical Resistance (R) resisting charge flow, measured in Ohms (Ω); Depends directly on length (l), inversely on cross-sectional area (A), and material resistivity (ρ): R = ρ(l/A)
Resistors in Series: Equivalent resistance Rs = R1 + R2 + R3; Same current flows through each resistor, while total voltage divides (V = V1 + V2 + V3)
Resistors in Parallel: Equivalent reciprocal resistance 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3; Same voltage across each branch, while total current divides (I = I1 + I2 + I3)
Joule's Law of Heating: Heat generated H = I^2 Rt = VIt = (V^2/R)t in a conductor
Practical applications of heating: Electric heaters, irons, tungsten filaments in incandescent bulbs, and protective electric fuses
Electric Power (P = VI = I^2 R = V^2/R), measured in Watts (W); Commercial electrical energy unit: kilowatt-hour (1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 Joules)

key_terms.definition: The rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor per unit time (I = Q/t).
The SI unit of electric current equivalent to one coulomb of charge flowing per second (1 A = 1 C/s).
The work done in moving a unit positive electric charge from one point to another in an electric circuit (V = W/Q).
The SI unit of electric potential difference equal to one joule of work done per coulomb of charge (1 V = 1 J/C).
Law stating that electric current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the potential difference across them at constant temperature.
The intrinsic property of a conductor that opposes the flow of electric current through it (R = V/I).
A characteristic material property representing resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area, measured in Ω·m.
Law stating that thermal energy generated in a resistor is proportional to the square of current, resistance, and flow time (H = I^2 Rt).
A safety device containing a low-melting-point wire connected in series to melt and break circuit during excessive current.
The rate at which electrical energy is consumed or dissipated in an electric circuit (P = VI).
The commercial unit of electrical energy equivalent to 3.6 × 10^6 Joules.

key_takeaways: Ammeters are always connected in series to measure circuit current; Voltmeters are connected in parallel to measure potential difference.
Resistivity of alloys is higher than constituent pure metals, making them ideal for heating appliance elements as they do not oxidise readily at high temperatures.
Series circuits are impractical for domestic lighting because failure of one component breaks the entire circuit, and different appliances require different currents.
Parallel circuits reduce equivalent resistance and ensure each appliance receives full supply voltage independently.
Fuses protect domestic circuits against overloading and short-circuiting by melting when current exceeds specified amperage ratings.
